title: Evidence-based practice
blurb: What evidence-based practice means, the hierarchy of evidence, trusted UK guidance and how to judge new products and techniques.
question: A sales rep visits the practice with a new surface disinfectant that "kills 99.9% of germs in seconds". A colleague wants to switch straight away. How would an evidence-based team decide whether to change, and where would you look for reliable evidence?

teach.body: Evidence-based practice means making decisions by combining the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's own values and preferences. It replaces "we've always done it this way" with "this is what the evidence shows works". The GDC expects you to keep your knowledge up to date and follow current best practice, and the Safe Practitioner Framework expects an evidence-based approach from every registrant.

teach.h: Three ingredients of an evidence-based decision
teach.caption: Leave out any one of the three and the decision is weaker. Research alone doesn't override what an informed patient wants.

teach.body: The higher up the pyramid, the lower the risk of bias. A systematic review gathers and combines all the good-quality studies on one question. A randomised controlled trial (RCT) puts patients into groups at random, so that the groups are alike and any difference is likely to be due to the treatment. Cohort studies follow groups over time, and case-control studies look back from an outcome. Case reports describe single patients, and expert opinion is a view without tested data.

Busy dental teams rarely read every study. Instead, they rely on guidance, where experts have already reviewed the evidence and turned it into recommendations. Key UK sources include NICE, the Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme (SDCEP), Delivering Better Oral Health (an evidence-based prevention toolkit), the Cochrane Library for systematic reviews, HTM 01-05 for decontamination and the BNF for medicines.

head: Source
Use it for
rows: National clinical guidelines, e.g. dental recall intervals
Practical dental guidance, e.g. prescribing and emergency drugs
Prevention advice by age and risk
Decontamination in primary care dental practices

teach.body: Manufacturers' claims, adverts and social media posts are not strong evidence. Before changing a product or technique, ask: who produced this evidence, and do they gain from it? Is it independent and peer-reviewed? How strong is the study type? Is it recent and relevant to UK practice? Does national guidance support it? Then think about the training, cost and workflow changes the new item brings, and follow the manufacturer's instructions for use once it is adopted.

teach.h: The five steps of evidence-based practice

steps.label: Assess
steps.sub: Did it work? Audit the results

teach.text: A sales leaflet, a colleague's habit or one impressive case is not high-level evidence. Systematic reviews sit at the top of the pyramid; expert opinion sits at the bottom.

items: Evidence-based practice = best research evidence + clinical expertise + patient values.
Hierarchy (strongest first): systematic reviews, RCTs, cohort, case-control, case reports, expert opinion.
RCTs randomise patients to reduce bias.
Use trusted guidance: NICE, SDCEP, Delivering Better Oral Health, Cochrane, HTM 01-05, BNF.
Appraise claims: who produced it, how strong, how recent, is it independent?

summary: You can now define evidence-based practice, rank types of evidence from systematic reviews to expert opinion, explain why randomisation reduces bias, name trusted UK guidance sources, and evaluate a new product or technique before the practice adopts it.

options: Doing what the most senior dentist prefers
Combining research, expertise and patient values
Following manufacturer leaflets for every choice
Always using the newest techniques available
A.why: Evidence-based practice combines the best research evidence with clinical expertise and the patient's values.

whyNot.0: Seniority isn't evidence; habits can be out of date.
whyNot.2: Manufacturers' leaflets may be biased and aren't the whole picture.
whyNot.3: New doesn't automatically mean better; it needs evidence.

A.q: Which type of evidence sits at the top of the hierarchy of evidence?
options: Expert opinion
Case reports
Systematic reviews
Case-control studies
A.why: Systematic reviews (and meta-analyses) combine all good-quality studies on a question, giving the strongest evidence.

whyNot.0: Expert opinion is at the bottom of the hierarchy.
whyNot.1: Case reports describe individual patients and are low in the hierarchy.
whyNot.3: Case-control studies are useful but rank below cohort studies, RCTs and systematic reviews.

A.q: A sales rep says a new disinfectant 'kills 99.9% of germs in seconds'. What should the practice do before switching?
options: Check independent evidence and guidance
Switch straight away, as it sounds better
Ask patients which product they prefer
Buy it only if it is the cheapest option
A.why: Marketing claims need checking against independent evidence and national guidance before practice changes.

whyNot.1: A claim from the seller isn't independent evidence.
whyNot.2: Patients' preferences matter for their care, but they can't judge disinfectant efficacy.
whyNot.3: Cost matters, but effectiveness and safety come first.

B.q: In a randomised controlled trial, why are patients allocated to groups at random?
options: To make the study finish more quickly
So patients can choose their own group
To avoid the need for patient consent
To reduce bias when comparing treatments
B.why: Random allocation makes the groups alike, so differences in outcome are likely to be due to the treatment and not bias.

whyNot.0: Randomisation doesn't speed up a study.
whyNot.1: Choosing your own group is the opposite of randomisation.
whyNot.2: Participants in trials must still give consent.

B.q: Which UK publication is an evidence-based toolkit giving prevention advice to dental teams?
options: The Data Protection Act
Delivering Better Oral Health
The Health and Safety at Work Act
The GDC's annual report
B.why: Delivering Better Oral Health is the evidence-based toolkit for prevention used by UK dental teams.

whyNot.0: The Data Protection Act is about personal data, not clinical prevention.
whyNot.2: This Act covers workplace health and safety duties.
whyNot.3: The GDC's annual report describes the regulator's work, not prevention advice.

B.q: A colleague uses an old technique because 'we've always done it this way', but national guidance has changed. What is the evidence-based response?
options: Follow the colleague, as they're more experienced
Use whichever method is quickest that day
Follow current guidance and discuss the change
Let each nurse decide for themselves
B.why: Practice should follow current evidence-based guidance; discussing it helps the whole team update.

whyNot.1: Speed isn't a measure of effectiveness or safety.
whyNot.3: Individual choices lead to inconsistent and possibly unsafe practice.

C.q: Which is the weakest form of evidence in the hierarchy?
options: Randomised controlled trial
Expert opinion
Cohort study
Systematic review
C.why: Expert opinion sits at the bottom of the hierarchy because it isn't based on tested data.

whyNot.0: RCTs are near the top of the hierarchy.
whyNot.2: Cohort studies rank above case reports and expert opinion.
whyNot.3: Systematic reviews are the strongest form of evidence.

C.q: Where would a dental nurse look for systematic reviews on oral health treatments?
options: A manufacturer's brochure
A social media forum
A colleague's revision notes
The Cochrane Library
C.why: The Cochrane Library publishes systematic reviews, including many on oral health treatments.

whyNot.0: Brochures promote products and may be biased.
whyNot.1: Social media posts aren't peer-reviewed evidence.
whyNot.2: Personal notes may be out of date and aren't reviewed evidence.

C.q: The practice is considering a new intraoral scanner. Which question best evaluates its impact on dental nurse practice?
options: What training and evidence support its use?
Does it look more modern than the old one?
Is it the brand a nearby practice uses?
Will it look good on the practice website?
C.why: Evaluating new technology means looking at the evidence for it and the training and workflow changes it brings.

whyNot.1: Appearance doesn't tell you whether it improves care.
whyNot.3: Marketing value isn't a clinical reason to adopt it.

reteach.title: Choosing a hotel
reteach.question: You're booking a holiday hotel. Do you trust one friend's opinion, a couple of online reviews, or a summary of thousands of verified reviews? Why?

blocks.h: More, fairer evidence beats one opinion
blocks.body: One friend's opinion is like expert opinion: useful, but it could just be their taste. A couple of reviews are like case reports: real, but maybe unusual. A fair comparison of guests split at random between two hotels is like an RCT. A summary that combines every reliable comparison is like a systematic review. The more evidence, and the fairer the way it was collected, the more you can trust it.

explain.body: Evidence-based decisions combine the best research evidence, the team's clinical expertise and the patient's values and preferences.

test.q: A patient declines a treatment that research supports. In evidence-based practice, how is this handled?
options: The research overrides her wishes
The nurse persuades her to agree
Her values are part of the decision
Treatment goes ahead as originally planned
test.why: Patient values and preferences are one of the three parts of evidence-based practice.

whyNot.0: Research doesn't override an informed patient's choice.
whyNot.3: Treatment without valid consent is never acceptable.

explain.body: Systematic reviews, then RCTs, then cohort, case-control, case reports and finally expert opinion. Higher levels have less risk of bias.

test.q: Which type of evidence is stronger than a cohort study?
options: A case-control study
A series of case reports
A randomised controlled trial
Expert opinion from a specialist
test.why: RCTs sit above cohort studies because randomisation reduces bias.

whyNot.0: Case-control studies rank below cohort studies.
whyNot.1: Case reports and case series rank below cohort studies.
whyNot.3: Expert opinion is the lowest level, however senior the expert.

explain.body: Guidelines turn evidence into practical recommendations. UK dental teams use NICE, SDCEP, Delivering Better Oral Health, Cochrane, HTM 01-05 and the BNF.

test.q: Which organisation produces practical guidance for dental teams, such as drug prescribing for dentistry?
options: NEBDN
CQC
HSE
SDCEP
test.why: The Scottish Dental Clinical Effectiveness Programme (SDCEP) publishes practical dental guidance, including Drug Prescribing for Dentistry.

whyNot.0: NEBDN is an awarding body for dental nurse qualifications.
whyNot.1: The CQC regulates and inspects care services in England; it doesn't write prescribing guidance.
whyNot.2: The HSE regulates workplace health and safety, not dental prescribing.

explain.body: Ask who produced the evidence and whether they gain, whether it is independent and peer-reviewed, how strong the study type is, how recent it is and whether guidance supports it.

test.q: Which question is most useful when appraising a study about a new product?
options: Is the report well designed and easy to read?
Who funded it, and do they gain?
Has it been shared widely on social media?
Does the company offer a free trial?
test.why: Knowing who funded a study helps you judge whether it might be biased.

whyNot.0: Presentation doesn't affect the strength of evidence.
whyNot.2: Popularity online isn't a measure of quality.
whyNot.3: A free trial is a sales offer; it tells you nothing about effectiveness.
